Chart themes

Source: vignettes/themes.Rmd
themes.Rmd

Start from a clean R session

Run each example separately in a fresh R session. They all plot stopping distance against speed using datasets::cars, which ships with R.

Default. Omitting the theme uses the package default in a fresh session.

library(highcharter)

hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist))

Preset for one chart. Carbon supplies its colors, grid and IBM Plex Sans.

library(highcharter)

hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist)) |>
  hc_add_theme(hc_theme("carbon"))

Preset for subsequent charts. Set the theme before creating the first widget. A later call to hc_set_theme() affects charts created after it.

library(highcharter)

hc_set_theme("carbon")
hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist))

Custom theme with a bundled font. Select IBM Plex Sans by name even when starting from an empty theme.

library(highcharter)

team <- hc_theme(
  colors = c("#005F73", "#CA6702"),
  chart = list(style = list(fontFamily = "IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif"))
)
hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist)) |>
  hc_add_theme(team)

System font. Keep Carbon’s colors and let the operating system choose the typeface. Each viewer sees their own system font.

library(highcharter)

team <- hc_theme("carbon", chart = list(style = list(fontFamily = "system-ui")))
hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist)) |>
  hc_add_theme(team)

Use an external font

Set fontFamily to a CSS family name to use a font supplied by the page or device. To bring a font with the theme, use sass::font_google(). The same theme works with hc_add_theme() and hc_set_theme().

Use a font supplied by the viewer or page. With a plain family name, the browser uses Noto Sans where available and sans-serif elsewhere.

library(highcharter)

team <- hc_theme(
  chart = list(style = list(fontFamily = "Noto Sans, sans-serif"))
)
hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist)) |>
  hc_add_theme(team)

Include Noto Sans with the chart. With the default local = TRUE, preparing the font requires an internet connection on the first download. The exported chart can then use the included files offline.

library(highcharter)

team <- hc_theme(
  chart = list(
    style = list(fontFamily = sass::font_google("Noto Sans"))
  )
)
hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist)) |>
  hc_add_theme(team)

Load Noto Sans from Google when the chart opens. With local = FALSE, the viewer needs a connection to Google Fonts. This example sets the custom theme for subsequent charts.

library(highcharter)

team <- hc_theme(
  chart = list(
    style = list(fontFamily = sass::font_google("Noto Sans", local = FALSE))
  )
)
hc_set_theme(team)
hchart(datasets::cars, "scatter", hcaes(x = speed, y = dist))

Choose a theme

The following gallery uses monthly sales for two regions. Set a default at the top of the script. Each widget captures it when you create the chart.

library(highcharter)

hc_set_theme("ft")

sales_chart <- function(...) {
  highchart(height = 260, ...) |>
    hc_title(text = "Monthly sales") |>
    hc_xAxis(categories = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun")) |>
    hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Units")) |>
    hc_add_series(name = "North", data = c(14, 17, 15, 21, 23, 24)) |>
    hc_add_series(name = "South", data = c(12, 14, 16, 17, 17, 20))
}

sales_chart()

To change a single chart, pass a theme to highchart(theme = ...) when constructing it, or apply one to an existing widget.

sales_chart() |> hc_add_theme(hc_theme("economist"))

Create a theme in R

A theme accepts the same option names as Highcharts. Start from scratch or override specific fields of a preset. For example, changing the colors below preserves Carbon’s typography, background and gridlines.

team <- hc_theme(
  colors = c("#005F73", "#CA6702"),
  title = list(align = "left"),
  chart = list(backgroundColor = "transparent")
)

team_carbon <- hc_theme("carbon", colors = team$colors)
hc_set_theme(team_carbon)
sales_chart()

Use hc_theme_merge(hc_theme("carbon"), team) to reuse all of the options in team. Nested fields merge by name. A supplied array replaces the previous array, so a two-color palette stays two colors long.

Use system fonts with a preset

To keep Carbon’s palette and gridlines while using the device’s interface font, override chart.style.fontFamily. A system font needs no web font files.

carbon_system <- hc_theme(
  "carbon",
  chart = list(style = list(fontFamily = "system-ui, sans-serif"))
)

sales_chart(theme = carbon_system)

Carbon’s title, axis labels and legend inherit this font. Other presets can set fonts on individual elements. For example, to change the title in hcrt, also set title = list(style = list(fontFamily = "system-ui, sans-serif")). The bundled theme fonts include the Latin subset, including Spanish accents. For other scripts the browser can use an installed font, or you can request a family explicitly with sass::font_google("Noto Sans KR").

Inherit a Shiny app’s theme

Switch the observatory between daylight and night. The sunspot series changes from copper to amber, and the axes, gridlines and tooltip follow the page. The chart uses the app’s serif typeface in both modes. Open Solar cycles in a new tab.

Set hc_set_theme("bslib") once at app startup. With Bootstrap 5.3, the first series inherits the primary color and the transparent chart background lets the page show through. Additional series use a categorical palette that you can replace with hc_colors().

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(highcharter)

observations <- window(sunspot.month, start = c(1950, 1), end = c(2019, 12))
annual <- aggregate(observations, nfrequency = 1, FUN = mean)
sunspots <- data.frame(
  year = as.integer(time(annual)),
  count = as.numeric(annual)
)

hc_set_theme("bslib")
observatory <- bs_theme(
  version = 5,
  bg = "#FFF4DE",
  fg = "#38261F",
  primary = "#9C3C16",
  base_font = "Georgia, serif"
) |>
  bs_add_rules(
    "
    [data-bs-theme='dark'] {
      --bs-body-bg: #101D30;
      --bs-body-color: #F3E6CD;
      --bs-primary: #FFBC65;
      --bs-border-color: #40516A;
    }
  "
  )

ui <- page_fluid(
  theme = observatory,
  style = "max-width: 48rem;",
  title = "Solar cycles",
  div(
    class = "d-flex justify-content-end align-items-center gap-2 py-2",
    "Color mode",
    input_dark_mode(mode = "light")
  ),
  highchartOutput("cycles", height = "320px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$cycles <- renderHighchart({
    hchart(
      sunspots,
      "area",
      hcaes(x = year, y = count),
      name = "Annual mean",
      fillOpacity = 0.18,
      marker = list(enabled = FALSE)
    ) |>
      hc_title(text = "Solar cycles, 1950–2019") |>
      hc_xAxis(
        title = list(text = NULL),
        labels = list(format = "{value:.0f}")
      ) |>
      hc_yAxis(min = 0, title = list(text = "Mean sunspot number")) |>
      hc_legend(enabled = FALSE) |>
      hc_tooltip(headerFormat = "<b>{point.x:.0f}</b><br/>", valueDecimals = 1)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

If the project uses a _brand.yml, put the same choices there and use theme = bs_theme(version = 5, brand = TRUE). The chart takes the values that bslib applies to the page. A standalone HTML widget uses the preset’s fallback colors and system font.

color:
  primary: "#783356"
typography:
  base: Georgia

In a multi-user Shiny app, apply per-user choices with hc_add_theme(hc_theme(input$preset)) inside renderHighchart(). The setter changes an R process option shared by its sessions.

The collection

Choose a preset below; every theme uses the same sales data. The chart is resized when its panel becomes visible.

  • 538
  • alone
  • bloom
  • bslib
  • carbon
  • chalk
  • cloudscape
  • darkunica
  • db
  • economist
  • elementary
  • ffx
  • flat
  • flatdark
  • ft
  • ggplot2
  • google
  • gridlight
  • handdrawn
  • hcrt
  • monokai
  • null
  • sandsignika
  • smpl
  • sparkline_vb
  • sparkline
  • superheroes
  • tufte

Use hc_themes() to list the available preset names.

The FT adaptation uses its web paper color and categorical line palette. Its separate bar palette applies to bars and columns with colorByPoint = TRUE. For several bar series, pass hc_theme("ft")$plotOptions$bar$colors to hc_colors(). The Economist adaptation uses dark and light blue as its first two series. Carbon uses IBM’s categorical sequence and blue sequential scale for maps and heatmaps. The editorial presets are highcharter adaptations. FT chart colors · The Economist on chart colors · IBM Carbon palettes.

For a Carbon map of changes around zero, use a symmetric range and set the neutral color at the midpoint. Reversing the signs would reverse the interpretation of the two ends of this scale.

change_theme <- hc_theme(
  "carbon",
  colorAxis = list(
    min = -10,
    max = 10,
    stops = list(list(0, "#491D8B"), list(0.5, "#FFFFFF"), list(1, "#004144"))
  )
)

Use hc_set_theme("cloudscape") for the light AWS Cloudscape chart palette. The ten series colors follow the order in its Highcharts components. The preset also uses Open Sans, a transparent background and rounded columns. Like the Carbon preset, this adaptation draws gridlines on both axes and uses circles wherever a series displays point markers. Cloudscape chart colors · Cloudscape chart styles.

The 538 and bloom presets preserve highcharter’s historical FiveThirtyEight and Bloomberg Graphics palettes. The darkunica, gridlight and sandsignika presets follow the themes shipped with Highcharts 12.6.0.

Tufte uses a gray palette, the Cardo font and small y-axis ticks, leaving the plotting area open.

The remaining presets use the same sales data, except for the compact single-series sparkline examples. The white area in sparkline_vb is shown on a teal value-box background. The chalkboard, paper and sand textures are embedded in the widgets and work offline.

Migrate an existing script

Replace hc_theme_ft() with hc_theme("ft"). A previous call to options(highcharter.theme = hc_theme_ft()) becomes hc_set_theme("ft"). The collection contains 28 presets, including db (Dotabuff), ffx (Firefox), elementary (elementary OS) and google (Google Books Ngram Viewer). To reproduce the former tufte2 style on a column chart, add an x-axis baseline and draw white gridlines over the columns.

bars <- hc_theme(
  "tufte",
  xAxis = list(lineWidth = 1, lineColor = "#737373", tickWidth = 0),
  yAxis = list(
    lineWidth = 1,
    tickWidth = 0,
    gridLineColor = "white",
    gridZIndex = 4
  )
)
sales_chart() |> hc_chart(type = "column") |> hc_add_theme(bars)
